title: Proxy pattern
idea: The Proxy pattern puts a stand-in with the same interface in front of a real object, to control creation, access rights or caching.

analogy.text: A receptionist answers for a busy director. They check who you are, answer common questions themselves, and only fetch the director when needed.
analogy.breaks: A proxy has the exact interface of the real object; a receptionist does not.

points: Virtual proxies delay creation, protection proxies check rights, caching proxies reuse earlier results.
Decorator adds features you stack; Proxy controls access; Adapter changes the interface itself.
`java.lang.reflect.Proxy` builds interface proxies; Spring wraps `@Transactional` beans in JDK or CGLIB proxies.
A call the real object makes on `this` skips the proxy entirely.

messages.label: get(q1) as ivy
messages.note: The caller holds a `Reports`. It cannot tell a proxy from the real thing.

messages.label: SecurityException
messages.note: Protection: ivy is not an analyst, so the call stops. The warehouse is never even created.

messages.label: get(q1) as ana
messages.note: An analyst asks for the same report. The proxy allows it.

messages.label: new Warehouse()
messages.note: Virtual: the expensive connection is made now, on the first allowed call, not at startup.

messages.label: get(q1)
messages.note: The proxy forwards the exact call it received.

messages.label: report q1
messages.note: The proxy stores the result before passing it back.

messages.label: report q1
messages.note: The caller gets the same answer the real object gave.

messages.label: get(q1) again
messages.note: Caching: the second request for q1 arrives.

messages.label: report q1 (cache hit)
messages.note: The proxy answers from its cache. The warehouse does no work.

code.title: A hand-written proxy
code.caption: One proxy class that checks rights, connects lazily and caches results.

walk.text: The subject interface and the real subject. Its constructor is the expensive part.
The proxy implements the same interface and holds a factory, not a live object.
Protection first: a denied caller costs nothing and never triggers the connection.
Caching next: a repeat request is answered without touching the real object.
Virtual last: the real object is built on the first miss, then reused.
`synchronized` makes lazy creation and the `HashMap` cache safe across threads.
Callers build the proxy and only ever see `Reports`; swapping it in changes no caller code.

code.title: JDK dynamic proxy
code.caption: The JDK generates the proxy class at runtime. Note what the audit does not see.

walk.text: One `InvocationHandler` receives every interface call, with the `Method` and its arguments.
Reflection wraps thrown exceptions; rethrow the cause, or callers get `UndeclaredThrowableException` instead.
`newProxyInstance` creates a class implementing the interface. It only works for interfaces.
`basket` calls `price` on `this`, the real object, so those inner calls skip the proxy.
The output shows one audit line for `basket`, not three. Spring self-invocation fails the same way.
The original `IllegalArgumentException` reaches the caller unchanged.

pitfalls: Calling a `@Transactional` method from its own class skips the proxy; its transaction settings are ignored.
A proxy around a cheap object with no access rules only adds indirection; call it directly.
A lazy proxy without synchronisation can create the real object twice under concurrent first calls.

quiz.q: With the classes from the dynamic proxy demo, how many lines starting with `audit:` does this print?
quiz.why: Each call on the proxy is audited once. The two `price` calls inside `basket` go through `this`, so they skip the handler.

takeaway: A proxy keeps the interface and decides whether, when and how calls happen.
